subject: Clarify TLS terminator ownership for on-prem gateway and private FQDN provisioning
messages:
From: Sarah Cole <sarah@acmehealth.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
Date: 2028-11-09T09:12:00-05:00
Subject: Help: TLS termination & private FQDN for our on-prem gateway

Hi Jonas,

Quick intro — I'm Sarah (Head of Platform at Acme Health). We're preparing a short POC to integrate Redwood Private into our on-prem environment next week. Two open questions that are blocking our infra team: 

1) Where should TLS terminate for traffic destined to the Redwood runtime? We currently terminate TLS at our F5 load balancers and use internal mTLS to upstream services.
2) How should we provision the private FQDNs for the Redwood endpoints? We have an internal DNS managed by Active Directory and would prefer not to publish anything publicly.

Attached is a simple network diagram (acme_onprem_network.pdf).

We'd like to understand recommended patterns from Redwood for private domains, whether you require public SANs or if split-horizon/internal CA is sufficient, and what the delegation/CSR workflow looks like.

Timeline: POC starts 2028-11-16, so any guidance by EOD 2028-11-10 would be hugely helpful.

Thanks,
Sarah
Sarah Cole
Head of Platform, Acme Health
(sarah@acmehealth.com)

From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Help: TLS termination & private FQDN for our on-prem gateway

Hi Sarah — thanks for the diagram and clear timeline. High level: Redwood supports two production-safe patterns for private deployments; I'll summarize and list concrete action items so your NetOps team can move forward quickly.

Option A — Customer-edge TLS termination (recommended when customer needs full control):
- Your F5 terminates public client TLS, performs any WAF inspection, then opens an internal mTLS session to the Redwood Private runtime (Redwood side expects client auth).
- DNS: Use split-horizon or private hosted zone so the Redwood endpoint FQDN resolves to internal IPs in your VPC/AD DNS.
- Certs: Customer provides certs (either public CA certs or internally signed certs) for the edge; Redwood can accept client cert validation with your CA chain.
- Pros: customer retains key control and audit trail; easier for regulated environments.
- Cons: requires customer to manage rotation and ensure compatibility with Redwood's client auth.

Option B — Redwood-managed termination (useful for teams that want us to own cert lifecycle):
- Redwood terminates TLS at a controlled ingress (within your VPC or on-prem sidecar) then routes to our runtime over mTLS internally.
- DNS: We need a zone delegation or conditional forward so that our provisioning systems can create the private records inside your DNS (or create a private hosted zone if permitted).
- Certs: We can generate CSRs, sign via a customer-provided internal CA or use a public CA where appropriate, and deliver certs to the on-prem termination point.
- Pros: reduces customer ops; Redwood automates rotation.
- Cons: requires trust exchange, KMS integration choices, and SOC 2 evidence for cert access.

Concrete action items for the POC:
1) Please confirm which option you prefer (A or B).
2) If Option A: provide the desired FQDN(s) and CA bundle for client verification + rotation window (example: 90 days).
3) If Option B: provide DNS admin contact and whether you can do a zone delegation (NS records) or accept conditional forwarding. We've seen AD DNS delegation via a subdomain (e.g., private.acme.example) work well.
4) NetOps contact for certificate/key delivery and whether you allow a Redwood provisioning host to create records in a private zone.

I'm attaching our brief pattern doc (redwood_tls_options.md) with a matrix of tradeoffs. If useful I can set a 30-minute tech sync today.

Thanks,
Jonas
Jonas Weber

Subject: Re: Help: TLS termination & private FQDN for our on-prem gateway

Jonas / Sarah — NetOps here. A few constraints from our side when integrating with internal AD DNS: 

- We cannot create records in the primary ad.acme.internal zone without an internal change request; preferred approach is to delegate a subdomain (redwood.acme.internal) to the Redwood name servers (split-horizon) or use conditional forwarders to a Redwood DNS view.
- We do not allow public CNAMEs that point to internal IPs; if Redwood needs to serve a single FQDN externally, we will front it with an external VIP and then rewrite internally.
- For certificate automation: we can accept CSRs and sign them with our internal CA (via an automated plumbing), or you can ship certs via secure SFTP to our ops account. 

Please note: if Redwood requires OCSP stapling and public revocation checks, we will need to confirm outbound rules from our DMZ to Redwood endpoints.

I've attached a short list of DNS options we maintain (netops-dns-options.txt).

Regards,
NetOps Team
netops@netops.example

Subject: Re: Help: TLS termination & private FQDN for our on-prem gateway

Adding a security ops perspective — thanks for the clear options, Jonas and NetOps. A few must-haves from compliance: 

- Key custody: For Option A (customer-edge termination) we require a formally documented key custody proof and rotation cadence that we can reference in our SOC 2 runbook. For Option B (Redwood-managed), we will only accept access to keys via a customer-managed KMS (HSM-backed) or via sealed transports; plain-text key transfer is not acceptable.
- Audit logs: Certificate issuance/rotation events must be available to both parties for 13 months (we can sync via S3 + CloudTrail-style logs or a signed log bundle).
- Rotation window: prefer 60-90 day cert TTL for PII-facing endpoints; if Acme requires longer we need explicit approval and compensating controls.
- Trust anchor distribution: confirm whether Acme can distribute our internal CA trust anchor to their clients/devices, or if you need public CA-signed leaf certs for client compatibility.

If Acme is constrained on AD delegation, Option A with customer-managed certs + our client-auth check is the faster route.

Karthik Iyer
Security Lead, Redwood Inference
karthik_iyer@redwood.ai

Thanks all — consensus on our side: start the POC with Option A (customer-edge termination) so we retain key custody and avoid DNS delegation changes during the short POC window.

Action items we'll take this week:
- NetOps to provide the CA bundle and an SFTP endpoint for cert delivery (NetOps: can you confirm by EOD 2028-11-10?).
- Acme will provide the FQDN list (wildcard vs SAN decision: we will provide SANs for the POC) and rotation window (we'll target 90 days).
- Jonas / Redwood to provide an explicit client-auth verification spec and expected CSR structure for our certs.

We have also attached a PO stub to confirm the POC (acme_po_stub.pdf) — we'll finalise procurement after the POC.

If that works I'd like to schedule the 30-minute sync Jonas suggested for 2028-11-13 to finalize the CSR and rotation steps.

Best,
Sarah
